questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Counting feature values that post-date their own event
questions.learningObjective: count the feature values admitted by a point-in-time mistake
questions.practice: production systems and applied case work
questions.stem: Training rows are built by pairing each account event with a thirty-day label window, and every row carries forty features. The features are joined on the label window's end date rather than on the event's own date, so a nightly-refreshed feature can be read up to seven days after the event it is attached to. Of 2,500 training rows, 1,600 have an event date at least seven days before their own window ends. How many feature values across the table did not exist at the timestamp of the event they are attached to?
questions.explanation: Each of the 1,600 late rows contributes forty feature values, so 1,600 times 40 is 64,000. The same figure comes from the complement: the table holds 2,500 times 40, which is 100,000 feature values, the 900 clean rows contribute 900 times 40, which is 36,000, and 100,000 minus 36,000 is 64,000 again. That is 64 per cent of every feature value in the training set, which is the number that should worry a reader: a majority of the inputs to the model describe a moment later than the moment being predicted. The tempting wrong answers are 1,600, which counts rows rather than values and understates the exposure by a factor of forty, and 100,000, which assumes every row leaks and so describes a different, wholly broken join.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of affected rows by the number of features each row carries, then check by subtracting the clean rows from all rows.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Precision at a score threshold on an imbalanced set
questions.learningObjective: compute precision from a confusion table at a chosen threshold
questions.practice: production systems and applied case work
questions.stem: At a score threshold of 0.5 a model is run over one thousand labelled cases and produces 60 true positives, 20 false positives, 140 false negatives and 780 true negatives. What is the precision at this threshold?
questions.explanation: Precision is the share of the model's positive calls that are right, so 60 divided by the 60 plus 20 it flagged is 60 over 80, which is 0.75, and the same figure is one minus the 20 over 80 that were wrong. The other numbers in the table explain why this item exists. Accuracy is 840 over 1,000, or 0.84, and it looks like the better result while describing a model that misses seven of every ten actual positives. Recall is 60 over 200, or 0.30, and dividing all correct calls by all cases instead of by the positives gives 0.06, a precision-looking number that is really the overall hit rate. The one figure that balances the two is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, which is 0.43 here and is the number to report when neither error is free.
questions.hint: Divide the true positives by everything the model called positive, which is the true positives plus the false positives.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What raising a threshold saves under a cost matrix
questions.learningObjective: compute the cost change produced by moving a decision threshold
questions.practice: production systems and applied case work
questions.stem: Across one thousand cases a low threshold gives 30 true positives, 270 false positives, 170 false negatives and 530 true negatives, while a high threshold gives 10 true positives, 20 false positives, 190 false negatives and 780 true negatives. A false positive costs 30 to have a person confirm it and a false negative costs 250 as a case that was missed. What is the total cost saved by moving to the high threshold?
questions.explanation: At the low threshold the cost is 270 times 30 plus 170 times 250, which is 8,100 plus 42,500, or 50,600. At the high threshold it is 20 times 30 plus 190 times 250, which is 600 plus 47,500, or 48,100. The saving is 2,500, and the change-of-state route reaches the same number without computing either total: raising the threshold removes 250 false positives, which saves 7,500, and adds 20 false negatives, which costs 5,000, so the net is 7,500 minus 5,000. The result is worth pausing on, because the high threshold detects 20 fewer real cases and still wins, which is the entire argument for a cost matrix. A threshold picked to maximise accuracy would have chosen the low one and been wrong by 250, and any threshold picked to maximise recall would have gone further in the same direction.
questions.hint: Cost each confusion count at its stated price, subtract the two totals, and then recheck by counting only the cases that changed.

questions.topic: A stability index computed from banded shares
questions.learningObjective: compute a population stability index from training and current band shares
questions.practice: production systems and applied case work
questions.stem: A model is monitored by banding its score into three ranges. The training shares of those ranges are 0.50, 0.30 and 0.20, and the shares in recent live traffic are 0.40, 0.30 and 0.30. The stability index sums, over the bands, the current share minus the training share multiplied by the logarithm of the current share divided by the training share. Rounded to three decimal places, what is the index?
questions.explanation: The top band contributes minus 0.10 times the logarithm of 0.8, which is 0.0223; the middle band is unchanged and contributes exactly nothing; the bottom band contributes 0.10 times the logarithm of 1.5, which is 0.0405. The sum is 0.06286, which rounds to 0.063. Splitting the sum into the two cross-entropy terms, the current shares weighted by their own log ratios less the training shares weighted by the same log ratios, returns 0.03238 plus 0.03048, which is the same 0.06286 reached by a different grouping. Note that every band contributes at or above zero, which is a property of the formula and a useful check: a negative term means the shares were entered the wrong way round. Adding up the absolute band movements instead gives 0.20 and answers a different question, and the largest single movement of 0.10 throws away the fact that the two shifts differ in size.
questions.hint: Take each band's share difference, multiply by the log of the ratio of shares, and add the three products.

questions.stem: A recommendation model is served at 09:00, but its feature table was rebuilt at 03:00 and the serving query reads the table exactly as it stood at 03:00. A user clicked at 08:15, and that click appears in neither the features nor the training data. Which requirement has this design broken?

options.text: Freshness, because the features handed to the model must describe the moment being scored rather than the last moment at which a batch happened to finish
Throughput, because a table rebuilt once a day cannot possibly keep pace with the number of clicks that arrive during it
options.misconception: blames processing capacity for a deliberate staleness choice

options.text: Reproducibility, because a serving query that does not return the same rows twice has not been pinned down to a fixed state
options.misconception: reports staleness as a failure of reproducibility

options.text: Coverage, because the click is absent from the table and so the case cannot be scored at all until it is rebuilt
options.misconception: reads a missing recent event as a case that cannot be scored

questions.explanation: The model is asked about 08:15 and answered about 03:00, and nothing about that substitution is visible at serving time because the query succeeded and returned a complete row. Freshness is a property with a stated deadline, and a batch job needs one written into its contract precisely because a successful query reports nothing about age. The other options misplace the fault: throughput is a question about how fast work is done rather than about when it starts, a repeatable snapshot is reproducible and stale at the same time, and a missing recent click is exactly the case that a recommendation system exists to handle, which is why the feature has to be as fresh as the decision.
questions.hint: Ask what time the features describe compared with the time the model is asked about.

options.text: Its sources of variation, since identical code on identical inputs must give identical outputs, and anything that moves is a source of randomness left unfixed
The training code itself, because code that gives two different answers cannot have been the same code on both occasions
options.misconception: concludes the two runs used different code

options.text: The processor, because machines round in different ways and therefore always fit a slightly different model
options.misconception: attributes every run-to-run difference to the hardware

options.text: The definition of the evaluation metric, because a score that moves between runs must have been computed two different ways
options.misconception: blames a change in the reported metric for a change in the fitted model

The colleague's controls matched, so the variation is coming from one of the unrecorded parts, and the honest first step is to record them rather than to pick a suspect. The other options each settle too early. Floating-point differences between machines are real but tiny, and they cannot explain a visible change in scores; a changed metric would change a reported number without changing the model, which is the reverse of what is described here.

options.text: A recent training window is still being revised upward, so a model fitted on it has been measured against labels that have not finished arriving
The window can simply be cut shorter until the labels are complete, which removes the delay from the problem rather than from the report
options.misconception: believes a shorter window removes an unsettled-label problem

options.text: Nine days is the figure to plan the cut around, since the median is the delay that half of all cases fall below
options.misconception: takes a median delay as the one that sizes a window

options.text: Every case is late by the same amount, because a distribution of delays is a description of one shared lag seen from different angles
options.misconception: reads a spread of delays as a single fixed lag

Any window cut at a fixed date therefore includes a tail of cases that are still unlabelled and will later be labelled positive, which inflates every performance figure computed inside it and makes the most recent data the most flattering data. questions.stem: A churn model is fitted on a table built by taking every account that was still open on the first of January, so closed accounts never appear in the file at all. What does this support?

options.text: The training set holds no examples of the outcome being predicted, and the rows it does hold were selected precisely for still being open
Nothing, provided the model is later scored on the same open accounts, since the training and scoring populations then match each other
options.misconception: believes matching the two populations settles a selection problem

options.text: A model that will under-predict churn, because the accounts that closed are absent and so can never raise the estimate
options.misconception: fixes a direction for the error from the absence of cases

options.text: An unbiased sample, because every open account is included and the ones left out are merely unrecorded rather than chosen
options.misconception: treats a census of survivors as unbiased sampling

questions.stem: Two ways of assembling training rows are on the table. Which pairing of join key and label window survives scrutiny?

options.text: Join the features as they stood at the event's own timestamp, and take the label from a window that opens at the event and looks only forward from it
Join the features as they stood at the label window's end date, since that is the date on which the finished row is written to the training table
options.misconception: joins on the date the row is written rather than the date it describes

options.text: Join the features as they stood at the event's own timestamp, and take the label from the whole account history so no genuine signal is discarded

options.text: Join the features as they stood one day before the label window ends, which is late enough to capture every feature that could ever have mattered
options.misconception: believes a join close to the label date is automatically a clean join

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a shadow deployment cannot establish
questions.learningObjective: explain what a shadow evaluation can and cannot establish about a candidate model
questions.practice: production systems and applied case work
questions.stem: Explain what a shadow deployment of a candidate model can and cannot establish about the candidate, and give the sentence that gets the limitation wrong.

answer.exemplar: A shadow deployment runs the candidate on live traffic in parallel with the incumbent, logs what it would have said, and throws the answer away. That establishes a good deal: that the candidate runs at real volume and real latency, that it survives the awkward rows the test set never contained, that its score distribution on today's traffic resembles the one it was validated on, and how often it disagrees with the incumbent and by how much. What it cannot establish is any difference in outcome, because nothing downstream of the decision changes. No one acts on the shadow's answer, so no customer is contacted differently, no loss is avoided and no revenue is affected, and every comparison of results is a comparison of two scores rather than of two worlds. The sentence that gets this wrong is the one that says the candidate's shadow score was higher than the incumbent's, so the switch is an improvement. A score is a prediction of an outcome, not the outcome, and comparing two predictions tells you about agreement rather than about benefit. A related wrong sentence claims the shadow period was a trial, which imports the idea that the traffic itself was exposed to the treatment; it was not, and calling it a trial is how a team talks itself into skipping the test that would have answered the question.

questions.explanation: The value of a shadow is that it converts engineering unknowns into measured facts at zero risk, and the limit is that it holds the consequence fixed while varying the decision. A useful discipline is to write down in advance what evidence would count as a reason to proceed, because a shadow produces a great deal of output and the temptation is to read improvement into whichever comparison was not pre-registered. The comparison a shadow genuinely supports is behavioural: how often the candidate would have acted, on whom, and how that lines up with what the business was already doing.
questions.hint: Ask whether anything downstream of the candidate's answer changed, and what that rules out.

questions.stem: A scorer reviews one event stream of 200,000 events a day and sends 0.4 per cent of them to a person, who spends 12 minutes on each. A reviewer is counted as a full-time equivalent for eight hours of handling a day. How many full-time equivalents does the queue need?

The same figure comes from the capacity side: a reviewer working eight hours handles 480 minutes, so 40 reviews a day, and 800 divided by 40 is 20. The unit is where this question is usually lost. Reporting 800 counts the work rather than the people, 160 counts the hours rather than the people, and treating 0.4 per cent as 0.4 per thousand gives 8,000 reviews and a hundred people, a tenfold error that a reader cannot see without redoing the percentage. The figure is also the smallest defensible one: it assumes perfect queueing, no absence, no training time and no rework, and a real service needs a margin on top of it.

questions.stem: A scoring gate refuses a daily partition whose required column is more than one per cent null. Over seven days the daily null counts on 120,000 rows each are 1,100, 1,300, 1,200, 1,450, 1,050, 1,600 and 980. How many of the seven partitions does the gate refuse?
questions.explanation: One per cent of 120,000 is 1,200, and the rule is stricter than that limit, so only the days above 1,200 are refused: 1,300, 1,450 and 1,600, which is three. The day with exactly 1,200 nulls sits on the boundary and is let through, and that single day is the whole difficulty of the item. A gate written as one per cent or more would refuse four partitions instead of three, so a threshold expressed with the wrong inequality is a production decision with a measurable cost. The other counts are below the limit and pass comfortably, including the 980 that a reader skimming for the largest number would not notice is the smallest. The useful practice is to test the boundary case explicitly, because a gate that is never exercised exactly at its limit is a gate whose behaviour there has never been decided.
questions.hint: Work out the row count that equals one per cent, then count the days strictly above it.

questions.stem: Retraining is triggered when a daily error figure exceeds 12 on two consecutive days, and the streak counter is only cleared after three consecutive days at or below 12. The ten daily figures are 9, 14, 13, 10, 11, 15, 16, 9, 10 and 9. On which day does the trigger fire for the first time?
questions.explanation: Day 1 is 9, day 2 is 14 and day 3 is 13, so day 3 completes the two-day run above 12 and the trigger fires there. Answering 2 names the first breach rather than the fire, and the whole purpose of the persistence rule is that one bad day should not trigger a rebuild. The reset rule then shapes what follows, and it is easy to miss: after the firing the counter needs three consecutive days at or below 12 to clear, and days 4 and 5 supply only two before day 6 breaks the run, so the counter is still live on day 6. Days 6 and 7 are 15 and 16 and fire a second time, which is what a reset keyed to a single good day would have prevented. A rule that triggers on the first breach produces a rebuild every time the metric wobbles, and a rule that never resets produces one rebuild per run of bad days forever.
questions.hint: Find the first pair of consecutive figures above the limit, then check whether the reset rule had cleared in between.

That the reported total is correct, because a currency column that has been renamed still holds amounts in the same unit as the rows above it

options.text: That the figure is 210,000 and therefore conservative, because adding a smaller number of large rows and more rows of small ones happens to offset the conversion

answer.exemplar: The intended-use section names the population the model was built for, the decisions it may inform, the conditions under which its performance figures hold, and the uses it was not evaluated for, and it is the section a later reader should read before acting rather than after. Its job is to make misuse a visible mismatch rather than a silent one, because almost every serious failure of a deployed model comes from a well-behaved model applied outside the range where it was measured. The sentence that gets it wrong is this one: the model may be used wherever a prediction of this kind is useful. It sounds like a permission and is in fact an abandonment, because a prediction of this kind covers inputs, populations and decisions that differ in exactly the respects the evaluation held fixed. A second wrong sentence names no population at all and describes the intended use purely as a workflow step, which protects the author from nothing, since the question that matters is who the model is pointed at and on what basis.

questions.explanation: A model card is read by two audiences with different needs, and the intended-use section serves both by fixing the boundary of the evidence. The performance figures in the same document are conditional statements, and the section is the condition; strip it out and the remaining numbers read as general claims about the model rather than as measurements on a particular population at a particular time. The practical consequence is that a change of use should require re-evaluation, and a card that cannot tell you whether the proposed use is inside its boundary leaves nobody able to say so.
questions.hint: Ask what the performance figures in the same document are conditional on.

questions.explanation: Each arm holds 20,000 users, and a proportion near 0.04 has a variance of about 0.0384 once the failure share is included, which over 20,000 users gives about 0.0000019 each, so the two sum to about 0.0000039 and the square root is 0.0020, that is 0.20 percentage points. Pooling the two arms before taking the variance gives the same figure to three places, which is the expected agreement and a useful check. The observed difference is 0.2 percentage points, which is about one standard error, so the honest reading is that the comparison has not yet distinguished the two arms rather than that they are equal. A standard error of 0.14 computed from the treated arm alone is the smaller and more flattering figure and it is wrong, because the control arm's sampling variation is part of the difference. Separating a fifth of a point on 20,000 users a side would take on the order of 150,000 a side, which is the number that tells a team whether the test is worth running at all.

answer.exemplar: Comparing the rate at which a model acts on two groups exposes a difference in the treatment the model hands out, and the exposure is genuinely informative because the difference is a property of the model rather than of the world. What it does not do is say which rate is right, and that is where the sentence that gets it wrong appears: the model is unfair because the rates differ. The two groups may differ in ways that make equal rates the wrong target, such as differing in the prevalence of the condition the model is screening for, in which case equal treatment rates would be equalising something that is not equal. A second wrong sentence picks the other direction and says the model is fair because the rates are close, which confuses a measurement with a verdict and lets a small gap pass unremarked while a large one is investigated. The defensible position is that a gap is a fact requiring an explanation, that the explanation is written down, and that the chosen target is defended as a policy decision by the people accountable for it rather than derived from the metric.

Each choice of metric, equal rates of a favourable outcome, equal error rates, equal calibration, makes a different group of people better and worse off, and the metrics are not simultaneously satisfiable in general, which is why reporting one without naming the others it displaces is a partial report. The operational habit that helps is to fix the metric before looking, to report the gap with its size, and to require an account of the gap rather than a declaration about the model.

The chance that the two systems see different users, since blending the lists guarantees both systems are exposed to the same traffic

options.text: The cost of the experiment, because a blended list needs only one system to render rather than two shown side by side
options.misconception: treats an experiment design as a cost question

That nothing about the table can be learned from the model, since a guarantee about one record at a time must generalise to any number of them

options.misconception: reads a training-set guarantee as covering neighbouring models

Work out the sensitivity of each answer, since an answer that changes by a hundred when one record moves needs far more budget than one that changes by one
Split the total budget across the answers in proportion to that sensitivity, so no single release can spend more than its share
Publish the noise scale beside each released figure and keep the record of what was spent, since a budget nobody accounts for is a budget nobody enforces

questions.explanation: The purpose comes first because a budget allocated before anybody has said what the answers are for will be spent on whatever was easiest to compute, and the purpose is what decides the sensitivity that follows. Sensitivity comes next and is the parameter that governs everything else, since the noise scale is the sensitivity divided by the allotted privacy parameter and a single dominant record can raise the sensitivity of a supposedly harmless count by orders of magnitude. The split has to be explicit because composition is cumulative: two releases that are each within budget can together exceed it, which is why the shares are fixed before any of them is computed rather than negotiated afterwards. Publishing the scale and keeping the record is what makes the allocation auditable, and an unlogged budget is indistinguishable from no budget at all once the second release has gone out.

questions.explanation: A quarter of one per cent of 2,000,000 is 5,000, so 5,000 rows short is the exact boundary and anything beyond it trips the gate. The second system is 10,000 short, which is half of one per cent and twice the limit, so this partition is refused rather than accepted. The gate is worth the trouble because the two counts come from different code and a shortfall of this kind leaves no trace inside either system: the writer succeeded, the reader succeeded, and the only symptom is a training table with fewer rows than the business generated. The tempting wrong answer is the 5,000 that the gate permits, which is the headroom rather than the breach, and the general habit it belongs to is comparing two numbers whose agreement is being assumed rather than reconciled. A reconciliation that reports the gap is useful even when it is small, because a gap that moves week to week is the early signal.
questions.hint: Take the stated fraction of the larger count, and ask whether the actual shortfall is above or below it.

questions.topic: What a small-count suppression rule costs

questions.stem: A published table suppresses any cell whose count is below 5. A table of 40,000 records contains 12 records with a value of 1, and each of them contributes 1 to the total. What share of the total does the suppression rule remove?
questions.explanation: Twelve records out of 40,000 is 0.0003, which is 0.03 per cent of the records and, because each contributes 1, 0.03 per cent of the total. The privacy benefit is the point of the rule and the cost is small here, which is the usual relationship and the reason such rules are standard. The arithmetic is worth doing anyway because the cost is not always small: a table grouped finely enough to have many single-count cells can lose a large fraction of a total that is spread thinly, and a suppression rule applied to a dimension with heavy skew will fall entirely on the largest group. What the figure does not establish is that the rule is well chosen, since a threshold of 5 and a threshold of 20 give the same protection against a determined attacker only in a loose sense, and the difference between them is usually several times this cost. Suppression is a floor, not a proof.
questions.hint: Divide the number of suppressed records by the total, using the stated contribution of one each.

questions.stem: A batch job finishes without an error, writes a file, and reports success. The file turns out to be missing 60,000 of the day's 12,000,000 rows. What does the job's success report actually establish?

options.text: That the code ran to completion, which is a statement about the job's control flow and not about whether the data it produced is the data that was asked for
That the job is fit for purpose, since a job that reports success has by definition met the contract its operator defined for it
options.misconception: treats a self-reported success as a verified contract

options.text: That the shortfall is downstream, since a job cannot know how many rows it should have written and so cannot be responsible for the count
options.misconception: relieves the job of responsibility for the count it caused

options.text: That the source was at fault, because a job reading from a source that returned too few rows could not have written more than it received
options.misconception: assigns the fault without evidence

questions.explanation: A success report is evidence about the path the code took and nothing about the content of what it produced, because every check the job performs is one it can perform from inside its own process. That is the structural reason a reconciliation has to come from elsewhere: a count from the source, a checksum agreed with the producer, or a total carried forward from a prior stage that used different code. Silently short output is the failure mode that a schedule and an error log both look straight past.
questions.hint: Ask whether the check the job ran could have failed, given that the job also produced the number.

questions.stem: A training table is built by taking every event in the ninety days before a fixed cut date and recording whether the account had churned by the date the table was assembled. What has this design produced for the events closest to the cut?

options.text: A group whose labels are still arriving, so those events look like non-churn and the assembled table records fewer failures than have happened
A group whose labels are complete, since a fixed cut guarantees that every event in the window has had the same time to be observed
options.misconception: believes a shared cut date equalises observation time

options.text: A group whose labels are missing entirely, so the events near the cut are dropped rather than mislabelled as survivors
options.misconception: assumes the design drops what it cannot observe

options.text: A group whose labels are biased low in both directions, since a short window makes every event equally likely to have been missed
options.misconception: confuses censoring with symmetric noise

questions.explanation: Every event in the window has a different amount of time in which to be observed, and the events nearest the cut have almost none, so their labels are not negative facts but unrecorded ones. Nothing in the table distinguishes the two, and a model fitted on it learns that a long quiet spell predicts a negative, which is true for the well-observed events and systematically wrong for the recent ones. The consequence is a training set whose failure rate falls as the window narrows, so a model tuned on it is tuned on a mixture of populations. The cure is a maturation lag: leave a gap between the last event and the cut at least as long as the label takes to arrive, so that every event in the window has had the same chance to be confirmed. Assembling later is the same idea and is easier to arrange than a shorter window.
questions.hint: Ask how long an event near the cut has had to be observed, compared with one near the start.

questions.stem: An offline feature store is rebuilt nightly. Over thirty nights the job reports that it wrote 100 per cent of the expected rows, and over the same period a comparison against the serving path finds that 0.4 per cent of scored rows carry a feature value the two paths disagree about. What does this support?

options.text: That the two paths are nearly but not exactly consistent, since a write that completed says nothing about the value written and the comparison is the only thing measuring agreement
That the two paths are consistent, because a store that wrote every expected row has by construction written the values the serving path reads
options.misconception: infers value agreement from row counts

options.text: That the disagreement is a rounding artefact, since 0.4 per cent is too small a figure to represent a genuine difference in a definition
options.misconception: dismisses a small rate as necessarily immaterial

options.text: That the comparison is the unreliable measurement, because comparing two paths over live traffic introduces differences the offline path never sees
options.misconception: dismisses the comparison rather than the disagreement

questions.explanation: A write count is a statement about volume and the agreement between two paths is a statement about content, and the two are independent. Thirty nights of complete writes are entirely compatible with a definition that fills a missing value differently on the two sides, since both paths then produce the right number of rows with the wrong values in a fraction of them. The comparison is the only instrument here that could see it, which is why it is run on a schedule and why its output belongs on a dashboard rather than in a one-off investigation. What matters operationally is that the rate is measured per feature, since a 0.4 per cent average can be one feature wrong on every row.
questions.hint: Ask what a row count establishes, and what a value comparison establishes.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a reliability claim has to survive
questions.learningObjective: explain what a stated reliability figure commits a service to
questions.practice: production systems and applied case work
questions.stem: Explain what a stated reliability figure commits a service to, and give the sentence that gets it wrong.

answer.exemplar: A reliability figure is a commitment about a rate over a window under stated conditions, and the whole of its force is in the three qualifiers: the rate says how often, the window says over what period, and the conditions say while what else was true. Read that way it is a falsifiable claim that an incident log can contradict, which is exactly its value, because a service that states one and then cannot reproduce it from its own records has learned something important about a promise it was making in writing. The sentence that gets it wrong is this one: the service is reliable, since it has not been down. Absence of a recorded outage is not availability, since the failures that matter are frequently partial, such as stale inputs, degraded accuracy or a queue that backs up, and a system that answers every request with a wrong answer has an availability figure of one and a usefulness of approximately none. A second wrong sentence treats the figure as a property of the past rather than as a promise about the future, which is how a good quarter becomes a standard the following quarter is measured against.

questions.explanation: A reliability claim is a distributional statement, and its three qualifiers are what make it checkable. Recording the numerator and the denominator, and keeping them per failure mode rather than pooled, is what lets anyone recompute the figure later from the same records. The habits that keep a claim honest are unglamorous: publish the figure with its window, publish the exclusions, and keep the incident log complete enough that the figure can be reconstructed from it.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would need in order to check the claim, and what its own records would have to contain.

options.misconception: treats a guardrail as a second reading of the same thing

options.text: To decide the sample size, since the guardrail is the metric with more observations and so determines how long the test must run

options.text: The endpoint's ability to serve its legitimate traffic, since a defence that throttles the whole endpoint to the level of the attacker also throttles the customers and simply converts the attack into an outage
The caller's ability to keep querying, since a rate limit that is visible and generous discourages abuse more effectively than a hard cut-off does
options.misconception: suggests a visible limit deters rather than bounds

options.text: The extractor's difficulty, because every additional obstacle between an attacker and a substitute model is worth more than any volume limit at all
options.misconception: puts obstacle count above protecting the service

options.text: The ability to detect the attack later, because a caller that is refused learns nothing and a caller that is served slowly leaves a trace the investigation can use
options.misconception: values traceability over protecting the service

questions.explanation: The attacker's interest is in a large number of scored inputs, and the defender's first obligation is to everyone else, so the constraint has to be applied per caller and the legitimate traffic has to be measured to make sure the per-caller rule is not catching it. A global limit is the failure this avoids, and it is a common one, because a global limit is the simplest thing to implement and it protects the model at the cost of the service. Slowing a caller rather than refusing it is a reasonable middle position, since the extractor's cost rises steeply while a legitimate integration sees no effect at all, but it is a mitigation and not a defence: enough queries still get through to be worth doing, and the defence that actually holds is not publishing the scores in a form that trains a substitute. Detection and rate limiting are complements rather than substitutes, and the ordering matters, because a defence that takes the service down has not defended anything.
questions.hint: Ask who bears the cost of the limit, and whether it is applied to the attacker or to everyone.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a re-run has to be able to assume
questions.learningObjective: identify what makes a batch job safe to run twice
questions.practice: production systems and applied case work
questions.stem: A batch job is re-run by hand after a failure, and it appends its output to a table that already holds a partial result from the first attempt. What property would have made the second run safe, and what is its absence costing now?

options.text: Idempotence, so that a second run replaces or recognises its own earlier output rather than adding to it, and its absence is now doubling a fraction of the rows
Atomicity, so that a failed run leaves nothing behind for a re-run to collide with, and its absence is what left the partial rows in place
options.misconception: conflates the absence of partial output with the safety of a re-run

options.text: Determinism, so that a re-run computes the same values, and its absence is why the two attempts disagree numerically
options.misconception: reads duplicate rows as a sign of differing values

options.text: Isolation, so that the two attempts cannot see each other's writes, and its absence is why the second pass overwrote the first
options.misconception: describes concurrent runs rather than sequential ones

questions.explanation: The two problems here are separate and only one of them is fatal. Atomicity is about failure, and a job that writes in one transaction leaves nothing behind when it dies, which is worth having and is not what makes a re-run safe. What makes a re-run safe is that it can be run again without consequence, which means the output is keyed so that a second execution overwrites or recognises its own earlier rows rather than appending beside them. Without that, every manual re-run is a data quality incident, and the damage is silent because the table still contains valid rows and every aggregate over it still returns a number. This is why the partition overwrite rather than the append is the setting people choose, and why the row count is the check that catches the mistake when the key is wrong.
questions.hint: Ask what a second execution does to the rows the first one wrote.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a stopping rule commits a test to
questions.learningObjective: state what a stopping rule commits a randomised test to
questions.practice: production systems and applied case work
questions.stem: A randomised comparison is watched daily and the team will stop when the outcome metric crosses a stated boundary. What has that stopping rule committed the test to?

options.text: A boundary fixed before any results were seen, since a rule chosen after the fact is a way of stopping at whatever point happens to suit the result
A fixed sample size, because a boundary that depends on the results cannot be converted into the number of users a plan requires
options.misconception: asserts that adaptive rules are impossible to plan around

options.text: Symmetry between the arms, since stopping early leaves the two arms with different numbers of users and so unbalances the comparison
options.misconception: believes an unequal final count unbalances a randomised comparison

options.text: A single decision, because a rule that stops on one crossing cannot also be used to continue when the result goes the other way
options.misconception: claims a boundary rule cannot handle either direction

questions.explanation: The commitment is that the boundary is chosen in advance, because the moment a result is visible, every reasonable-looking stopping point becomes available and the temptation to take the best one is overwhelming. A rule fixed beforehand can be inspected, argued with and costed, and it can be a boundary or a proper sequential method; what it cannot be is a number chosen afterwards. The other three are all avoidable. An adaptive rule can be sized in advance from the smallest effect worth detecting, an unequal final count is normal in any randomised comparison and unbalances nothing provided the assignment was random, and a boundary is applied symmetrically in either direction because a test that only stops on a favourable crossing is not a test.
questions.hint: Ask when the boundary was chosen relative to the first result being seen.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A store that has drifted from the path that reads it
questions.learningObjective: identify the mechanism by which an offline store creates skew
questions.practice: production systems and applied case work
questions.stem: Training features are materialised into an offline store at 02:00 each day from a snapshot taken at 01:00, and the serving path computes the same features live. On a feature that reads the current hour of day, the two disagree for every request between 01:00 and 02:00. What has the arrangement produced?

options.text: Skew that is confined to a time window and a specific feature, so a model can learn from the snapshot hour and meet a different value in production for the same reason
Skew that is unavoidable, since a materialised snapshot can never hold the same values as a live computation at any moment of the day
options.misconception: treats a snapshot as inherently unable to match

options.text: No skew at all, because both paths read the same source table and a difference in the moment of reading is not a difference in the value
options.misconception: assumes the two paths read the same instant

options.text: Skew that a shorter snapshot interval would remove, since a finer schedule makes the two moments closer without ever making them equal
options.misconception: conflates a smaller gap with no gap

questions.explanation: A feature whose value depends on when it is computed is a feature that will differ between a snapshot and a live read whenever the two moments differ, and no store design removes that for such a feature. The useful conclusion is narrower and more actionable than the general one: the skew is confined to a time window and to the features that read a clock, so the two things to do are to make those features read as of a fixed reference point and to measure the comparison on the window where they can differ. Finer snapshot intervals reduce the window without closing it, and treating the arrangement as safe because both paths read the same source is the mistake, since the source is read at two different times. The general rule is that a feature's definition should name the instant it is as of, and a feature that cannot name one will not agree across paths.
questions.hint: Ask which features depend on when they are read, and during which window the two paths can disagree.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A reliability claim the incident log does not support
questions.learningObjective: test a stated reliability figure against the service's own incident record
questions.practice: production systems and applied case work
questions.stem: A service reports 99.9 per cent availability for the quarter. Its incident log for the same quarter holds four entries: one twenty-one hour outage, two four-hour degradations in which scores were served from a stale table, and one ninety-minute period in which half the requests failed. What does this support?

options.text: That the figure is not supported by the log, since the four entries account for well over the roughly 2.2 hours a quarter at 99.9 per cent permits, and two of them are degradations a pure uptime measure would not count at all
That the figure is supported, since no entry records a full outage of more than a day and a day is well within a quarter's allowance
options.misconception: treats a quarter's allowance as roughly one day

options.text: That the log is the unreliable record, since incident entries are written by the people who were on call and are therefore biased toward the memorable
options.misconception: dismisses the record rather than the claim

options.text: That the figure is supported for the uptime it measures, and the two degradations belong in a separate availability measure rather than in this one
options.misconception: accepts a figure that excludes the reported degradations

questions.explanation: Ninety-nine point nine per cent of a quarter permits about 2.2 hours of unavailability, and the log's own entries sum to more than thirty, of which the 21 hour outage alone is an order of magnitude over. The deeper problem is the third option's subject, which is that a figure defined as pure uptime excludes the two degradations entirely, and a service that served stale scores for four hours was not available in any sense a customer would recognise. That is the reason the claim has to name its conditions: rate, window and what counts as a failure, and the habit of reporting availability alongside a measure of degraded service is what makes the two comparable. The second option mistakes the granularity of the measure for its scale, and the fourth is a proposal to redefine the term in a way that makes the claim true, which is a change to the metric rather than to the service.
questions.hint: Work out how much unavailability the stated rate permits in a quarter, and ask which entries that covers.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A drift statistic that fires on a change of no consequence
questions.learningObjective: interpret a drift alert against the outcome it was supposed to predict
questions.practice: production systems and applied case work
questions.stem: A drift detector reports a stability index of 0.31 on a feature, past a trigger of 0.25, for nine consecutive days. Over the same nine days the model's accuracy on held-out traffic is unchanged at 0.88, and the feature's distribution has not shifted again. What does this support?

options.text: That the alarm has fired without a consequence so far, so the question is whether the trigger should require persistence of the outcome as well as of the input
That the model is degrading, since a stability index past its trigger is by definition a signal that the model no longer fits the data it sees
options.misconception: treats an input alarm as proof of a model problem

options.text: That the detector is broken, because an index that has not moved further over nine days cannot be reporting a genuine change in the distribution
options.misconception: reads a stable reading as evidence the alarm is false

options.text: That the retraining should proceed regardless, because nine days past a trigger is a settled fact rather than a reading to be interpreted
options.misconception: treats a persistent alarm as self-justifying

questions.explanation: A drift statistic measures the input distribution and nothing else, so an alarm is a statement that the inputs have moved rather than that the model has stopped working, and a feature can move a long way in a direction the model handles perfectly. The nine days of unchanged accuracy are the reason to ask whether the trigger is set correctly rather than to conclude that the alarm is spurious: it has persisted, which is a real change, and it has had no effect, which is also a real fact, and a trigger that requires both would have spared nine days of investigation. The detector is not broken, since the flat reading is a stable index well past its threshold and the distribution has simply stopped moving. Retraining on the strength of the alarm alone is the most expensive of the four responses, and it is the one an escalating alert structure pushes a team towards.
questions.hint: Ask what the statistic measures, and what the outcome over the same period says about it.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a point-in-time join guarantees
questions.learningObjective: explain what a point-in-time join guarantees and the sentence that gets it wrong
questions.practice: production systems and applied case work
questions.stem: Explain what a point-in-time join guarantees about a training row, and give the sentence that gets it wrong.

answer.exemplar: A point-in-time join guarantees that every feature in the row carries the value it held at the instant the row is about, so the row describes what was knowable then rather than what the tables happen to contain now. That is a guarantee about information, not about correctness: the values it retrieves may be wrong, but they are the wrong values that were current, and a model fitted on them meets the same wrong values in production. The sentence that gets it wrong is this one: the join prevents leakage, so the score is honest. It prevents one kind of leakage, the kind that comes from reading a value written after the moment being predicted, and it does nothing about a feature that was current and already carried the answer, which is what a label rule written into a column looks like. A second wrong sentence says the join makes the training set representative of production, which confuses two different problems: a join controls the timing of the inputs and has no bearing on whether the population in the training table resembles the population being scored.

questions.explanation: The guarantee is temporal and worth stating in those terms, because the two failure modes are routinely confused. A future value read into a training row is a leak the join closes. A present value that happens to encode the outcome is a leak the join cannot see, and it is found by asking what the feature could tell a model about the label rather than by checking timestamps. The second failure is the more common one and the more expensive to discover in production.
questions.hint: Ask what the join controls, and then ask what it cannot see.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a drift detector can and cannot report
questions.learningObjective: explain what a drift detector can and cannot establish about a model
questions.practice: production systems and applied case work
questions.stem: Explain what a drift detector can and cannot establish about a model, and give the sentence that gets it wrong.

answer.exemplar: A drift detector establishes that the distribution of something has moved relative to a reference, and it establishes it without needing anybody to have looked at the outcome, which is what makes it worth running daily. It cannot establish that the model is worse, that the movement will persist, or that any particular action is the right response, and the gap between those two lists is where a monitoring programme either earns its keep or manufactures work. The sentence that gets it wrong is this one: drift is detected, so the model is retraining. The move from a measured distribution to a scheduled rebuild skips the step that matters, which is asking whether the move has changed what the model gets right, and skipping it produces a pipeline that retrains on a schedule set by an alarm while its accuracy quietly falls for a reason no input statistic would ever show. A second wrong sentence says no drift means the model is fine, which is the symmetric error and is answered by a trigger that watches the outcome as well as the inputs.

questions.explanation: A useful framing is that a detector measures a change and a decision needs a consequence, and the two are different measurements. The ones that change the inputs without changing the predictions are common, and the ones that damage the predictions without changing the inputs are rarer but real, which is why a detector is one instrument among several rather than the instrument.
questions.hint: Ask what the statistic measures, and what would have to be measured before acting on it.
